'''Robert Iain McLachlan''' {{post-nominals | country = NZL | FNZMS | FRSNZ | size = 85%}} (born 1964) is a [[New Zealand]] mathematician and Distinguished Professor in the School of Fundamental Sciences, [[Massey University]], New Zealand.<ref name="massey" /> His research in [[Geometric integrator|geometric integration]] encompasses both [[Pure mathematics|pure]] and [[applied mathematics]], modelling the structure of systems such as liquids, [[Climate variability|climate cycles]], and [[quantum mechanics]]. He also writes for the public on the subject of [[climate change policy]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=McLachlan |first=Robert |date=2025-01-21 |title=NZ's climate policies are no longer enough to keep warming at 1.5°C – here's what needs to happen |url=http://theconversation.com/nzs-climate-policies-are-no-longer-enough-to-keep-warming-at-1-5-c-heres-what-needs-to-happen-245829 |access-date=2025-07-03 |website=The Conversation }}</ref>

== Academic career ==
McLachlan was born in [[Christchurch]], New Zealand in 1964,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://id.loc.gov/authorities/names/no2003108628.html|title=McLachlan, Robert I. (Robert Iain), 1964–|website=LOC|access-date=20 April 2020}}</ref> and studied mathematics at the [[University of Canterbury]], graduating with a [[Bachelor of Science|BSc (Hons)]] First Class in 1984.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=van Brunt|first=Bruce|date=2013|title=Robert McLachlan|url=https://nzmathsoc.org.nz/downloads/profiles/NZMSprofile118_Robert_McLachlan.pdf?t=1378287401|journal=New Zealand Mathematical Society Newsletter|volume=118|pages=18–19}}</ref> One formative experience was in his last year of high school, where he had free rein to experiment with [[assembly language]] programming on the school [[PDP-11|PDP-11/10]].<ref name=":1" />

McLachlan went on to graduate work in numerical analysis in 1986. He received a PhD from [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] (the California Institute of Technology) in 1990, supervised by [[Herbert Keller]] in [[computational fluid dynamics]], with a thesis titled "Separated Viscous Flows via Multigrid".<ref name=":1" /> He then worked as a [[Postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral fellow]] at the [[University of Colorado Boulder]] in what was then the new field of [[symplectic geometry]]. After meeting [[Jürgen Moser]], who was visiting [[Boulder, Colorado|Boulder]] at the time, McLachlan spent six months on a postdoctoral fellowship in Switzerland, at the [[Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich]].<ref name=":1" />

McLachlan joined [[Massey University]] in [[Palmerston North]] in 1994, and began a collaboration with [[Reinout Quispel]] at [[La Trobe University]] that resulted in over 26 publications on geometric integration.<ref name=":1" /> In 2002 he became Professor of Applied Mathematics at Massey, and spent a year's sabbatical at the [[University of Geneva]], working with [[Gerhard Wanner]] and [[Ernst Hairer]], and the [[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters|Norwegian Academy of Sciences]] in Oslo.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Vlieg-Hulstman|first=Marijcke|date=April 2002|title=Massey University|journal=Newsletter of the New Zealand Mathematical Society|volume=84|page=10}}</ref> In 2007 he won the prestigious Germund Dahlquist Prize, the first mathematician from the southern hemisphere to do so.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|url=https://www.nzedge.com/news/maths-prize-for-massey-prof/|title=Maths Prize for Massey Prof|date=13 August 2007|website=NZEDGE|access-date=2020-04-16}}</ref> From 2008 to 2012, along with [[Stephen Marsland]] and [[Matthew Perlmutter|Matt Perlmutter]], he worked on a [[Marsden grant]] project "Geodesics in diffeomorphism groups: geometry and applications", designing efficient numerical integrators that preserved the geometric properties of systems.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Tuffley|first=Christopher|date=December 2009|title=Massey University|journal=Newsletter of the New Zealand Mathematical Society|volume=107|page=17}}</ref> In 2013, McLachlan was the LMS-NZMS Aitken Lecturer, delivering talks on geometric numerical integration to six UK universities.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.lms.ac.uk/events/lectures/forder-and-aitken-lectureship#Aitken|title=LMS-NZMS Forder and Aitken Lectureships|last=Fisher|first=Elizabeth|date=25 July 2019|website=London Mathematical Society}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.lms.ac.uk/sites/lms.ac.uk/files/Events/Aitken%20Lecturer%202013%20poster.pdf|title=LMS – NZMS Aitken UK Lecture Tour 2013|date=2013|website=London Mathematical Society}}</ref>

McLachlan is a Fellow of the [[New Zealand Mathematical Society]] (NZMS), and in 1998 organised the first of the annual Manawatu-Wellington Applied Mathematics Conferences. He was president of the NZMS in 2008–2009 and vice president in 2010, and edited the ''New Zealand Journal of Mathematics'' for six years.<ref name=":1" /> Since 2016 he has been a Distinguished Professor in Massey's School of Fundamental Sciences.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://sites.massey.ac.nz/rangahau2018/masseys-eminent-researchers/|title=Massey's eminent researchers|date=2018|website=Rangahau {{!}} Research at Massey University|access-date=2020-04-16}}</ref>

== Research ==
McLachlan is a world leader in the field of [[Geometric integrator|geometric integration]], a technique for the reliable simulation of large-scale complex systems, and in particular the use of [[Symplectic integrator|symplectic]] techniques in the numerical analysis of [[differential equation]]s.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=https://scientists.org.nz/Hill-Tinsley-Medal|title=New Zealand Association of Scientists – Hill Tinsley Medal|website=scientists.org.nz|access-date=2020-04-16|archive-date=3 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180803134242/https://scientists.org.nz/Hill-Tinsley-Medal|url-status=dead}}</ref> This field, which McLachlan helped found in the 1990s, builds into its approach the underlying geometric structure of data sets.<ref name=":0" /> Because it allows the simulation of large systems, it has the potential for solving practical problems in fields as disparate as the structure of liquids, [[Climate variability|climate cycles]], the motion of the [[Solar System|solar system]], particles in [[Particle accelerator|circular accelerators]], [[Chaos theory|chaos]] in dynamical systems, and weather forecasting.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2007-08/sfia-ma081307.php|title=Robert McLachlan awarded Germund Dahlquist Prize|last=Stephenson|first=Jessica|date=13 August 2007|website=EurekAlert!|publisher=AAAS|access-date=16 April 2020}}</ref> For example, during [[Hurricane Sandy]] in 2012, the [[European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts]], using geometric integration models, correctly predicted the hurricane would suddenly turn 90 degrees towards New York six days in advance.<ref name=":2" /> McLachlan's methods have been used in computational science to examine a possible celestial origin of the [[ice age]]s, biological models, and the dynamics of flexible structures.<ref name=":2" /> His research contributed to a solar system simulation that revised the dates of geophysical epochs by millions of years.<ref name=":0" /> Although his work in geometric numerical integration has a wide range of real-world applications, he considers himself a [[Pure mathematics|pure mathematician]].<ref name=":2" />

== Science communication ==
As an advocate for action on climate change McLachlan writes frequently for the public, in media like ''[[Scientific American]]''<nowiki/>'s blog,<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/observations/climate-change-is-a-fourfold-tragedy/|title=Climate Change Is a Fourfold Tragedy|last=McLachlan|first=Robert|date=4 June 2019|website=Scientific American Blog Network|access-date=2020-04-16}}</ref> the blog ''Planetary Ecology'' and the [[Royal Society Te Apārangi]]'s ''Sciblogs''. His writing focuses on [[effects of climate change|consequences of climate change]],<ref name=":3" /> the benefits of wind turbines,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://blog.planetaryecology.org/2019/12/19/blow-wind-of-fruitfulness/|title=Blow, wind of fruitfulness|last=McLachlan|first=Robert|date=19 December 2019|website=Planetary Ecology|access-date=16 April 2020}}</ref> electric cars,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://blog.planetaryecology.org/2019/12/28/should-i-ditch-my-fossil-fueled-car/|title=Should I ditch my fossil-fueled car?|last=McLachlan|first=Robert|date=28 December 2019|website=Planetary Ecology|access-date=16 April 2020}}</ref> and climate policy.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://blog.planetaryecology.org/2019/11/11/zero-carbon-its-not-just-a-good-idea-its-the-law/|title=Zero Carbon: it's not just a good idea, it's the law|last=McLachlan|first=Robert|date=11 November 2019|website=Planetary Ecology|access-date=16 April 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sciblogs.co.nz/climate-explained/2019/12/18/which-countries-are-likely-to-meet-their-paris-agreement-targets/|title=Which countries are likely to meet their Paris Agreement targets|last=McLachlan|first=Robert|date=18 December 2019|website=Sciblogs|access-date=2020-04-16}}</ref>
